title: Comet or cluster?
caption: The globular cluster Messier 62, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 62, NGC 6266 · constellation Ophiuchus · about 22000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, S. Anderson et al.

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Most globular clusters are nearly perfect spheres of stars, but Messier 62 is distorted. The 12-billion-year-old cluster stretches out on one side into a comet-like shape, with a bright head and an extended tail. It is one of the closest globulars to our galaxy's center, and strong tidal forces there likely pull many of its stars out of place.

Globular clusters tend to be denser toward their centers, and the more massive a cluster, the denser that center is likely to be. Weighing almost a million Suns, Messier 62 ranks among the densest globulars. Stars there interact and merge regularly, and huge stars burn out fast, explode, and leave behind white dwarfs, neutron stars and, sometimes, black holes.
For years, astronomers believed black holes would soon be kicked out of globular clusters. In 2013, though, one was found in Messier 62, the first in a Milky Way globular cluster.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.70 x 2.77 arcminutes) and distance (22000 light years), the frame spans roughly 17 × 18 light-years. Its light set out about 22,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This view combines ultraviolet and visible light from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet light is invisible to the human eye, and Hubble resolves stars in the cluster's dense core that an eye could not separate.
